rv.q: Hinds proves himself a master storyteller, weaving together memories with remarkable grace and authenticity.
This is a deeply honest and courageous work from an actor digging deep into what now matters to him.

Yes Despite the abundance of other projects, this polished but informal program (unobtrusively directed by Lonny Price) of personal anecdotes, private memories and rueful reflections on his life seems special.
And yet, the transition from page to stage feels undermotivated, incomplete.
Unfortunately, in this lusterless staging of “Walking with Ghosts,” there is little refuge.
And it is perhaps this very restraint that makes the telling all the more effective.
Connecting the dots between vignettes in a more powerful thematic way would give the show a cumulative wallop that now feels somewhat lacking.
“Walking With Ghosts” is a modest show, with quiet humor and gentle pathos — which is exactly why it’s so wonderful.

Only the actor’s gift for storytelling, with its surprising deftness at delineating the voices, brogues, and mannerisms of the multiple characters he portrays—a talent he too rarely gets to demonstrate in his stage and film roles—lift these familiar tropes to a level of compelling theatre.
In its best moments, “Walking with Ghosts” has a similar effect, leaving viewers entertained and a little haunted — and perhaps just a bit more appreciative of the wonder that life and art can bring.
Luckily, Byrne proves to be an appealing, often moving raconteur, keeping our attention for the somewhat overextended 2-hour and 20-minute running time, rarely indulging in mawkish sentimentality.

"Walking with Ghosts" is a decidedly intimate experience, one that seems tailor-made for an off-Broadway theater like the Irish Rep. Price and his production team try to expand the show to Broadway proportions through McKenna's lighting and aforementioned set and Sinéad Diskin's vivid sound design.
There is a convincing intimacy to Walking With Ghosts, but that intimacy is also slightly deceptive.

But what we are presented with, even as it is sparkled with Sinéad McKenna's supportive lighting design and Sinéad Diskin's original music and sound design, is both too much and not enough, a two-hour discourse that would best be appreciated by fans of the actor.
Fiennes is great, of course, but the play goes nowhere.
But you too often feel the actorly polish which ironically results in a distancing effect from the traumatic incidents being related.
But Walking With Ghosts moves in fits and starts, flickering with imagination before ultimately fading away in a ghostlike haze.
He’s an actor who needs a big role, and the Byrne of “Ghosts” is all too ephemeral, not to mention forgettable.
And everyone else gets to spend time, at least, with a man who has a clear capacity to love.
Walking With Ghosts is a gift that shouldn’t be missed.
Still, anyone who has yearned for a closer relationship with a father or a son may find themselves tearing up at the end.

cn.t: Gabriel Byrne's storytelling charm captivates in this intimate memoir adaptation, though critics split on whether his personal anecdotes justify a full Broadway production, with some finding it poetic and affecting, others deeming it overlong and unfocused.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
